input: Researchers at the University of Example have developed a new battery chemistry that stores nearly twice as much energy as conventional lithium-ion cells. The team replaced the graphite anode with a silicon-carbon composite and added an electrolyte additive that prevents the silicon from cracking as it swells during charging. In laboratory tests, prototype cells kept 90 percent of their capacity after 1,000 charge cycles. The authors say the materials are inexpensive and compatible with existing factories, but caution that the cells have so far only been tested at small scale and at room temperature. Electric-vehicle makers have expressed interest, and a pilot production line is planned for next year.
